content: Facilities at international, regional, national, and local levels must be equipped to address water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) in healthcare settings. Achieving the targets outlined in this report requires leadership and commitment across all levels of governance. Without such leadership, these goals will remain unattainable. Strong institutional leadership from the Ministry of Health and effective governance at national, sub-national, and facility levels are essential to implement the eight practical steps described in this document. However, the responsibility for WASH does not rest solely with the Ministry of Health. Ministries of Water and Sanitation play a critical role in improving municipal WASH supplies and providing technical expertise to healthcare facilities. Ministries of Finance are instrumental in allocating budgets and establishing financing mechanisms. Local governments are responsible for managing and funding WASH initiatives at the community level. Overall coordination requires leadership that transcends any single ministry to ensure a unified and cohesive approach. The President or Prime Minister’s Office should lead the development, funding, and implementation of a national roadmap for WASH in healthcare facilities. This includes working with the Ministry of Finance to allocate sufficient funds for operations, maintenance, and capital costs where feasible. Independent evaluations of WASH efforts should be supported, and national decrees, statements, and roundtables should be utilized to promote these initiatives. International, regional, and local health and development partners must provide global leadership, coordination, and technical support. They should align their efforts with national roadmaps, tools, and approaches, dedicating resources specifically to WASH in healthcare facilities. Financing institutions, philanthropic organizations, and donors should mobilize resources and invest in sustainable WASH services. The private sector should contribute by investing in innovative technologies and behavior change strategies to maintain services and improve practices. The Ministry of Health must commit to greater leadership, investments, and tracking of WASH initiatives, as outlined in the 2019 World Health Assembly Resolution on WASH in healthcare facilities. This resolution, unanimously approved by the 34-member states of the WHO Executive Board, calls for national assessments, roadmap development, target setting, and the implementation of standards. It aligns with global efforts and the eight practical steps for improving WASH services. The resolution will be voted on by all WHO Member States at the World Health Assembly in May 2019. Ethiopia’s Clean and Safe Health Facility (CASH) initiative, launched in 2014, exemplifies the impact of multi-level leadership. Triggered by a comment to the Ethiopian Minister of Health about poor WASH services, the initiative aims to reduce healthcare-associated infections and improve patient safety through infection prevention and control measures. High-level leadership has been critical to its success, with regional health bureaus supporting facilities, celebrities acting as ambassadors, and the private sector improving WASH infrastructure and services. At the facility level, ward managers encourage staff to embrace cleanliness under the slogan “Cleanliness is everybody’s responsibility.” Community engagement is fostered through town hall meetings and aesthetic improvements to facility landscaping. The CASH initiative has been implemented in all 150 national hospitals and is expanding to primary healthcare facilities. Over 150 individuals have been trained in infection prevention and control practices and WASH service management. However, challenges remain, including the sheer number of facilities and the need for sustainable funding from regular budgets. Ongoing audits aim to identify highand low-performing facilities and address specific operational, maintenance, and funding challenges. Cambodia’s National Health Strategic Plan 3 (HSP3) demonstrates how a situation analysis can embed WASH into health system and quality improvement plans. In 2015, the Ministry of Health recognized WASH as a priority and conducted a systems analysis to align partner activities with national priorities. This analysis identified existing data, policies, standards, and targets, as well as opportunities for strengthening policies and programming. It also assessed the government’s readiness for health policy reform. As a result, a baseline assessment of WASH conditions in 117 health facilities was completed, and WASH was included as an indicator of quality care. New standards and guidelines were adopted, and WASH practices were integrated into the curriculum for health center management training. Monitoring tools were contextualized and tested, and operational research on hygiene behavior and infection prevention practices during childbirth is underway. Lebanon’s national assessment of 166 primary healthcare centers (PHCCs) highlighted the need to include basic WASH requirements in national specifications and accreditation standards. New WASH standards and quality measures have been integrated into Lebanon’s Primary Care Accreditation Standards. Interim solutions, such as providing bottled drinking water, are being implemented while safe piped supplies are planned and installed. A national curriculum has been developed to ensure annual training for PHCC personnel on the importance of improved WASH services. Ghana’s national study on health and the environment revealed that over 90% of outpatient conditions could be prevented with appropriate environmental and health measures. WASH was identified as a critical determinant of health outcomes, leading to the development of national standards for WASH in healthcare facilities. These standards have improved the quality of care and reduced preventable conditions. In summary, achieving universal access to quality WASH services in healthcare facilities requires coordinated efforts across multiple sectors and levels of governance. Strong leadership, sustainable funding, and community engagement are essential to overcoming challenges and ensuring the success of these initiatives.
